blocks.content: Picture the last time you mailed something physical to another person. You did not just hand over a bare sheet of paper. You folded it into an envelope and wrote an address on the outside. That envelope may have gone inside a padded shipping box carrying a tracking label. The box then got loaded onto a delivery truck, which only needed to know which city and which depot to head towards, nothing about what was actually written on your letter.

Every layer of that packaging exists for a different, very specific reason, and none of the outer layers needs to know or care what the inner ones contain. This is precisely, mechanically, what happens to a piece of data crossing a computer network. This closing topic of the Networking Fundamentals module is where that exact mechanism gets its name, encapsulation on the way out, and decapsulation on the way back in.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867352-380240938.png
1. The Envelope, the Box, and the Truck
blocks.text: 1. The Envelope, the Box, and the Truck

blocks.content: Every earlier topic in this module built a piece of the picture you need for this one. The OSI and TCP/IP models gave you the idea of layers stacked on top of each other, each with a distinct job. How data travels showed you that data actually moves across a network broken into packets, handed from router to router. This topic is where those ideas fuse into one precise mechanical story, what physically happens to your data as it crosses each of those layers.

The postal analogy holds up well because it captures the one rule that makes the whole system work: each layer of packaging only understands its own layer. The envelope only needs a name and street address. The shipping box only needs a building and a tracking code. The truck only needs a city and a route. None of them need to open the layer beneath to do their job correctly, and that is exactly the property computer networks were designed around.

["The letter itself, the actual message you wrote, meant only for the recipient","The envelope, adds a name and street address, read by the local mail carrier","The shipping box, adds a building and tracking code, read by the shipping depot","The delivery truck, adds a route and destination city, read by the transport network"]
items: The letter itself, the actual message you wrote, meant only for the recipient
The envelope, adds a name and street address, read by the local mail carrier
The shipping box, adds a building and tracking code, read by the shipping depot
The delivery truck, adds a route and destination city, read by the transport network

blocks.title: Why the order matters
blocks.content: Notice the packaging is always added in the same order and removed in exactly the reverse order. You cannot open the shipping box before taking it off the truck, and you cannot read the letter before opening the envelope. Networks enforce this same strict, reversible order, and that order is exactly what encapsulation and decapsulation describe.
2. Encapsulation: What Happens on the Way Down
blocks.text: 2. Encapsulation: What Happens on the Way Down

blocks.content: Encapsulation is the process of wrapping data in a new header as it moves down through the network layers on the sending side. Using the four layer TCP/IP model from the sibling topic in this module, that means data moves from the Application layer, down through the Transport layer, down through the Internet layer, and finally down through the Network Access layer, picking up one new header at each stop.

Each header is added by exactly one layer, and that layer writes into it only the information it personally needs to do its job later. The layer doing the wrapping never looks inside the data it is wrapping. It treats everything handed down from the layer above, the original data plus any headers already added, as one opaque bundle, and simply adds its own header on the outside of that bundle.

This is a strict, disciplined process. By the time data reaches the bottom of the stack and is ready to go out onto the physical wire or radio signal, it is wearing four layers of packaging, one from each layer it passed through, in the exact order it passed through them.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867353-485772591.png
blocks.alt: Encapsulation: What Happens on the Way Down

blocks.content: 3. The Name Changes at Every Layer
blocks.text: 3. The Name Changes at Every Layer

blocks.content: Here is something that trips people up the first time they hear it: the wrapped bundle of data gets a completely different name depending on which layer just finished wrapping it. This is not just trivia. Engineers use these exact words constantly in real conversation, in documentation, and in tools like packet capture software, so it is worth learning precisely rather than approximately.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867353-901479719.png
blocks.alt: The Name Changes at Every Layer

blocks.content: {"headers":["Layer","Once wrapped, it is called","Added by"],"rows":[["Application","Data","The application itself, this is the starting point, nothing wrapped yet"],["Transport","Segment","The Transport layer, after adding its header"],["Internet","Packet","The Internet layer, after adding its header"],["Network Access","Frame","The Network Access layer, after adding its header"]]}

Notice the pattern. Data becomes a segment. A segment becomes a packet. A packet becomes a frame. Each of these words refers to one very specific stage, not to data in general, and mixing them up is one of the most common small mistakes beginners make, covered directly later in this topic.
4. What Each Header Actually Contains

Knowing the names is only half the picture. Each header is not just decoration, it carries specific fields that the layer which added it, and only that layer, needs to do its job. A brief look at what lives inside each header makes the whole system click into place, and each of these gets a full dedicated topic of its own later in the course.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867353-847399147.png

{"headers":["Header added at","Carries","Used for"],"rows":[["Transport layer","Source and destination port numbers","Identifying which specific application on each end the data belongs to"],["Internet layer","Source and destination IP addresses","Identifying which device on which network the data came from and where it is going"],["Network Access layer","Physical addressing for the local network hop, commonly a MAC address","Delivering the data across one physical link, such as one Ethernet or WiFi hop"]]}

blocks.title: Coming up in full depth
blocks.content: Port numbers and IP addressing are large enough topics that they each get their own dedicated chapter later in this course. For now, the important thing is knowing that each layer's header holds precisely the information that layer needs, nothing more.
5. Decapsulation: What Happens on the Way Up
blocks.text: 5. Decapsulation: What Happens on the Way Up

blocks.content: Decapsulation is the exact reverse of encapsulation, and it happens at the receiving end. As the frame arrives and moves up through the layers on the destination device, each layer strips off and reads exactly the one header that belongs to it, uses whatever information that header holds to decide what to do next, and passes the remaining content up to the layer above.

The Network Access layer strips its header first, since it was the last one added and therefore the first one encountered on the way back up. What remains is handed up as a packet. The Internet layer strips its header next, handing up a segment. The Transport layer strips its header last, and what finally arrives at the Application layer is the original data, byte for byte identical to what the sender's application first handed down.

This symmetry is not an accident, it is the entire point. Whatever order the headers were added in going down, they are removed in exactly the reverse order going up, the same way you cannot get to a letter without first opening the envelope you already removed from the box.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867354-784600015.png
blocks.alt: Decapsulation: What Happens on the Way Up

blocks.content: 6. Why Each Layer Minds Only Its Own Header
blocks.text: 6. Why Each Layer Minds Only Its Own Header

blocks.content: Here is the design principle that makes this whole system worth understanding deeply, not just memorizing. Every layer, at every device that touches the data along its journey, only ever needs to read the one header that belongs to it. It never needs to open, understand, or even know about headers belonging to other layers.

Take a router forwarding a packet across the internet. A router only needs to read the Internet layer header to decide which link to send the packet out on next. It does not look at the Transport layer header to see which port the data is headed for, and it certainly does not look inside at the actual application data, whether that is a webpage, a video call, or part of a file transfer. It reads one header, makes one forwarding decision, and moves on.

This separation of concerns is exactly what lets a single, shared network carry web traffic, video calls, and file transfers side by side, all at once, without every router needing to understand any of those applications specifically. The router does its job by reading exactly one layer of the packaging, precisely the way the delivery truck driver does not need to read your letter to get the truck to the right city.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867354-151455547.png
blocks.alt: Why Each Layer Minds Only Its Own Header

blocks.title: A genuinely important idea
blocks.content: This is one of the most useful ideas in all of networking. Layers stay independent of each other on purpose, so the network underneath never has to change just because a new kind of application gets invented on top of it.
7. A Complete Journey: Tracing One Message End to End
blocks.text: 7. A Complete Journey: Tracing One Message End to End

blocks.content: All of this becomes far more concrete with one worked example, tracing a single small piece of data through the entire encapsulation and decapsulation journey, layer by layer, with realistic example values at each stop.
Say your laptop sends a short chat message to a server, the word Hello, over a secure connection. Watch what gets added, and later removed, at every single step.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867354-587855157.png
blocks.alt: A Complete Journey: Tracing One Message End to End

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","What happens","Result"],"rows":[["1","The application hands over its raw data, the message Hello","Data"],["2","Transport layer adds a header with source port 51422 and destination port 443","Segment"],["3","Internet layer adds a header with source IP 192.168.1.12 and destination IP 142.250.183.14","Packet"],["4","Network Access layer adds a header with the local physical addressing for this hop","Frame"],["5","The frame travels across the network as electrical, light, or radio signals","Frame in transit"],["6","At the destination, the Network Access header is read and stripped","Packet"],["7","The Internet header is read and stripped","Segment"],["8","The Transport header is read and stripped","Data, exactly the original message Hello"]]}

Notice the destination ends up with precisely the same data the sender started with, unchanged, even though four separate headers were added and then removed along the way. That exact roundtrip, intact and unchanged, is the whole promise encapsulation and decapsulation exist to keep.

Keep this table close by as you move into the next topics on ports and IP addressing. Every time you hear the word segment, packet, or frame from here on, you will know exactly which layer, and which header, that word refers to.
9. Common Mistakes to Avoid
A couple of mix ups come up constantly once people start using this vocabulary in practice, and both are worth clearing up now rather than carrying forward as quiet confusion.

["Using segment, packet, and frame interchangeably, as if they all mean the same generic thing, when each one specifically refers to data wrapped at one particular layer","Calling something a packet before it has reached the Internet layer, or a frame before the Network Access header has actually been added","Assuming a router or switch needs to inspect the full contents of the data it forwards, when in reality it only ever reads its own relevant layer's header","Forgetting that decapsulation happens in exactly the reverse order of encapsulation, never the same order"]
items: Using segment, packet, and frame interchangeably, as if they all mean the same generic thing, when each one specifically refers to data wrapped at one particular layer
Calling something a packet before it has reached the Internet layer, or a frame before the Network Access header has actually been added
Assuming a router or switch needs to inspect the full contents of the data it forwards, when in reality it only ever reads its own relevant layer's header
Forgetting that decapsulation happens in exactly the reverse order of encapsulation, never the same order

blocks.title: A quick way to check yourself
blocks.content: If you are ever unsure which term to use, ask which layer just finished adding its header. Transport gives you a segment, Internet gives you a packet, Network Access gives you a frame. That one question resolves the confusion every time.
10. Key Takeaways
That closes out the Networking Fundamentals module, and this final topic is really the thread that ties every earlier one together into a single precise mechanical picture.
